274.title: Jnana yoga: neti neti in practice; Shankara's method; the Ashtavakra Gita opening (1 of 7)
274.hook: so, what do you do? the third path asks a harder question
274.tomorrow: Jnana yoga: neti neti in practice; Shankara's method; the Ashtavakra Gita opening (2 of 7)
274.howItsDone: In Vedanta, jnana yoga is practiced by studying the Upanishads with a teacher, reflecting on them, and meditating on the self as the witness of body and mind; 'not this, not this' (neti neti) is one of its classic tools.

segments.voice: Last week: bhakti yoga, and the line love as the road. Nine doors, the Tamil saints, Mira, Tulsidas, Surdas, and a street full of kirtan. Did you sing with someone? Today, the third path. Day two hundred seventy-four.

You're at a party, and someone you've just met asks the question. So, what do you do? And you answer. A job title. Maybe where you live, whether you have kids, what you studied. Now imagine they don't accept any of it. No, not your job. Who are you? You try your name. That's a label your parents picked. Your personality? That's changed a lot since you were eight. Your body? Most of it has been rebuilt since you were a child. Keep going, and it gets strange fast. The third path of yoga starts right there, at the question you can't quite answer.
screen: `SO, WHAT DO YOU DO?` → `NO: WHO ARE YOU?` → `THE QUESTION YOU CAN'T ANSWER.`

segments.voice: Jnana comes from the Sanskrit root jna, to know. It's a cousin of the English word know, and the Greek gnosis. But jnana doesn't mean information. You can't look it up. It means knowing the way you know you're awake: direct, from the inside. Karma yoga asked what you do. Bhakti asked who you love. Jnana asks who is doing and loving in the first place. One of the oldest teachers of this road is a sage in the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad named Yajnavalkya, and he gives it a tool with two words. Neti, neti. Not this, not this. When people asked him to describe the self, the real I, he refused to give it a label. Whatever you can point at, he said, is not it. Not the body. Not the breath. Not the thoughts, not the feelings. Not this. Not this. It sounds like a riddle, but the logic is simple. Anything you can observe is something you're observing. So it can't be the observer. Yajnavalkya puts it as a question elsewhere in the same Upanishad: by what would one know the knower? Your eye can see everything except itself. The jnana path, then, isn't a matter of adding knowledge. It's subtraction. Peeling off everything that turns out to be an object, until what's left is the one who was looking all along. This week we'll practice that peeling, meet the method of the great teacher Shankara, and open a strange, fierce little book called the Ashtavakra Gita. The line for the week is short: who am I?
screen: `JNA — TO KNOW, FROM THE INSIDE.` · `NETI, NETI: NOT THIS, NOT THIS.` · `WHO KNOWS THE KNOWER?` · `SUBTRACTION, NOT ADDITION.` · then, large: `WHO AM I?`

segments.voice: Sit, and try Yajnavalkya's two words, gently. Notice the weight of your body on the seat. Say inwardly: I notice this. So it's not quite me, not this. Notice the breath. Not this. Notice a thought pass through. Not this, either. Don't push anything away; just notice it's being noticed. Then rest for a moment as the one who's noticing, without trying to describe it. If it slips away, begin again. The bell holds the time.
Jnana yoga. The path of knowledge: not information, but knowing from the inside who you are. Its first tool is neti, neti, not this, not this.
Your line: who am I? Today, the next time someone asks what you do, answer them normally, and silently ask yourself the deeper question. Day two hundred seventy-four.

275.title: Jnana yoga: neti neti in practice; Shankara's method; the Ashtavakra Gita opening (2 of 7)
275.hook: ten travelers cross a river, count themselves, and find only nine
275.tomorrow: Jnana yoga: neti neti in practice; Shankara's method; the Ashtavakra Gita opening (3 of 7)
275.howItsDone: Advaita Vedanta teachers often use the parable of the tenth man to show that self-knowledge isn't gaining something new but recognizing what was always present; students then practice discerning the witness from what it witnesses.

segments.voice: Yesterday: jnana yoga, and Yajnavalkya's two words, neti, neti. Not this, not this. Your line: who am I? Did the question follow you around? Today, a story Vedanta teachers love. Day two hundred seventy-five.

Ten friends set out on a trip together, and they have to ford a fast river. They wade across, holding on to each other, and scramble up the far bank, soaked. The leader, to be safe, counts heads. One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine. Nine. He counts again. Nine. Someone's been swept away. Each of the others counts, and each of them gets nine too. They sit down on the riverbank and start to weep for their lost friend.
screen: `TEN FRIENDS CROSS A RIVER.` → `ONE, TWO… NINE.` → `THEY WEEP FOR THE LOST ONE.`

segments.voice: A traveler walking by asks what's wrong. They tell him: there were ten of us, and one has drowned. He looks at them, and counts. Ten. He asks the leader to count again. Nine. And then the traveler touches the leader on the shoulder and says: you are the tenth. That's the whole story. It's told in Advaita Vedanta texts, and teachers have used it for centuries, because it's exactly how neti neti works in practice. The leader wasn't missing. He was doing the counting, so he never counted himself. He was looking everywhere but at the looker. And notice something else. Nothing new was found. No one came out of the river. The grief ended the moment he recognized what had been there the whole time. That's why jnana is called knowledge, not achievement. You don't become the self. You stop leaving it out of the count. So how do you practice it? Neti neti in real life is a kind of honest sorting. When you feel, I am angry, look closer: anger is showing up, and something is aware of it. Not this. When you think, I am a failure, look closer: a thought is showing up. Not this. You don't deny the anger or the thought. You just stop counting them as the counter. And each time, what's left is the one who was looking. You are the tenth. The Upanishads have a phrase for this recognition, and later teachers repeat it again and again: you are that.
screen: `THE TRAVELER COUNTS: TEN.` · `YOU ARE THE TENTH.` · `NOTHING NEW WAS FOUND.` · `STOP LEAVING YOURSELF OUT.` · then, large: `WHO AM I?`

segments.voice: Sit, and count, like the leader on the riverbank. One: the body, sitting. Two: the breath. Three: a sound in the room. Four: a thought. Five: a feeling, whatever mood is here. Keep counting whatever shows up. Then pause, and ask: who's counting? Don't answer with a word. Just turn toward the counter, the way the traveler turned the leader around. Rest there. When counting starts again, let it. The bell holds the time.
Jnana yoga, in practice. Neti neti sets aside what can be counted, the body, the thoughts, the moods, and turns you toward the counter. You are the tenth.
Your line: who am I? Today, when you catch yourself saying I am tired, or I am annoyed, add silently: and something knows it. Day two hundred seventy-five.

fork.reveal: you are the tenth. the counter never counted himself.

what it means: in jnana yoga, nothing new is found; you recognize the knower who was always there.

what a scholar hears: the tenth-man parable (dashamas tvam asi) appears in Advaita works such as Shankara's Upadeshasahasri and Vidyaranya's Panchadashi (ch. 7); it echoes the Chandogya's tat tvam asi, 'you are that'.

276.title: Jnana yoga: neti neti in practice; Shankara's method; the Ashtavakra Gita opening (3 of 7)
276.hook: a husband offers to split the property; his wife asks for something else
276.tomorrow: Jnana yoga: neti neti in practice; Shankara's method; the Ashtavakra Gita opening (4 of 7)
276.howItsDone: In Advaita Vedanta, students traditionally study the Upanishads and Shankara's commentaries with a teacher (shravana), work through doubts and questions (manana), and then practice sustained contemplation (nididhyasana).

segments.voice: Yesterday: ten friends, a river, and the leader who forgot to count himself. You are the tenth. Your line: who am I? Did you catch the knower behind a mood? Day two hundred seventy-six.

The sage Yajnavalkya, the one who said neti neti, decides to leave home and live as a wandering monk. He has two wives, and he calls one of them, Maitreyi, to settle things. Let me divide what I have between you and Katyayani, he says. It's a fair, sensible offer. Maitreyi asks one question. If this whole earth, full of wealth, were mine, would it make me immortal? No, he says. Your life would be like the life of the rich. That's all. And she says: then what would I do with something that won't make me immortal? Tell me what you know instead.
screen: `LET ME DIVIDE WHAT I HAVE.` → `WOULD IT MAKE ME IMMORTAL?` → `TELL ME WHAT YOU KNOW INSTEAD.`

segments.voice: Yajnavalkya is delighted, and he teaches her. And in that conversation in the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, he gives a line that became the backbone of the jnana path. Paraphrased: the self is what should be seen. It should be heard about, reflected on, and deeply meditated on. Centuries later, the great teacher Shankara, in the eighth century or so, took those verbs and made them a method. Three steps, still taught in Vedanta schools today. First, shravana: hearing. You listen to the teaching, from the Upanishads and from a teacher, carefully, the way Maitreyi listened. Not skimming. Hearing. Second, manana: reflecting. You argue with what you've heard. You raise every doubt. Does this make sense? What about this objection? Shankara didn't want blind belief; he spent pages answering objections. Third, nididhyasana: deep, sustained meditation. Once the doubts have settled, you dwell on the teaching until it's no longer an idea you hold but the way you see. Hear it, test it, soak in it. It's how you learn anything that really changes you. You hear a friend say you're kinder than you think. You argue with it. And then, slowly, over months, you live into it. Shankara also insisted on a teacher. Not a guru to worship blindly, but someone who has walked the road and can point, like the traveler who turned the leader around. And notice where this began. Not with a scholar. With a woman who turned down half a fortune and asked for the truth.
screen: `MAITREYI TURNS DOWN THE FORTUNE.` · `SHRAVANA: HEARING.` · `MANANA: REFLECTING.` · `NIDIDHYASANA: SOAKING IN IT.` · then, large: `WHO AM I?`

segments.voice: Sit, and try the three steps with one small line. Here it is: I am aware. First, hear it. Just let the words land. Then reflect: is it true, right now? Is there awareness here? Test it honestly; raise any doubt you have. Then, if it holds, soak in it. Don't repeat the words. Rest in what they point to, the plain fact of being aware. The bell holds the time.
Jnana yoga, Shankara's method: shravana, manana, nididhyasana. Hearing the teaching, reflecting on it, and meditating on it until it becomes how you see.
Your line: who am I? Today, take one idea you've heard this week and argue with it, honestly, on a walk or in the shower. That's manana. Day two hundred seventy-six.

original.note: Sanskrit: hearing, reflecting, deep meditation — the three steps of Vedanta study.

trapdoor: what you thought: meditation is the whole of the knowledge path.
what it means: Shankara's method has three steps: hearing the teaching, reflecting on it, and meditating on it.

277.title: Jnana yoga: neti neti in practice; Shankara's method; the Ashtavakra Gita opening (4 of 7)
277.hook: on a narrow lane in Kashi, the great teacher tells a man to step aside, and the man asks who should move
277.tomorrow: Jnana yoga: neti neti in practice; Shankara's method; the Ashtavakra Gita opening (5 of 7)
277.howItsDone: Vedanta teachers traditionally describe four qualifications for students of self-knowledge (sadhana chatushtaya): discrimination, dispassion, the six virtues of a steady mind, and longing for freedom; students work on these alongside study.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Maitreyi, who turned down a fortune, and Shankara's three steps. Hearing, reflecting, soaking in it. Your line: who am I? Did you argue with an idea? Day two hundred seventy-seven.

There's a story told about Shankara in Varanasi, the holy city also called Kashi. He's walking to the river with his students, and on a narrow lane a man comes toward them with his dogs. A man from a community that the purity rules of the day kept at a distance. Shankara says what the custom said to say: move aside. And the man doesn't move. He asks: which should move away from which? This body from that body? Both are made of food. Or this self from that self? There's only one. Shankara, the story says, stopped, and bowed to him.
screen: `A NARROW LANE IN KASHI.` → `MOVE ASIDE.` → `WHICH SHOULD MOVE FROM WHICH?`

segments.voice: Tradition says Shankara then composed five verses, the Manisha Panchakam, each ending: whoever sees this way is my teacher, whatever his birth. It's a humbling story to find at the center of a great teacher's life, and that's partly why people tell it. Knowing the teaching isn't the same as living it. So what does it take to live it? Texts in Shankara's tradition, like the Vivekachudamani, list four qualifications a student needs. Not degrees. Qualities. First, viveka: discrimination, in the old sense. Telling the lasting from the passing. The body, the mood, the reputation: passing. What's aware of them: lasting. Second, vairagya: dispassion. Not hating the world, just loosening your grip on what passes. You still enjoy the meal; you just don't need it to save you. Third, six treasures of a steady mind. Calm. Self-restraint. Doing your own duty without fuss. Patience with heat and cold, praise and blame. Trust in the teacher and the teaching. And focus. Fourth, “mumukshutva”: longing for freedom. The texts say this one matters most. Without it, the others are just good habits. Think of Maitreyi turning down the fortune. That was “mumukshutva”. Think of Shankara bowing on the lane. That was viveka catching up with him: he saw that the rule was about bodies, and the one he'd been teaching about was not a body at all. The man with the dogs had it the whole time.
screen: `VIVEKA: LASTING FROM PASSING.` · `VAIRAGYA: LOOSENING THE GRIP.` · `SIX TREASURES OF A STEADY MIND.` · `THE LONGING TO BE FREE.` · then, large: `WHO AM I?`

segments.voice: Sit, and try viveka, gently sorting as things arise. A sound: passing. A twinge in the knee: passing. A worry about tomorrow: passing. A pleasant memory: passing too. Don't push any of it away. Just label it, softly, passing. Then notice what hasn't passed through all of it. The noticing. Rest there for a few breaths. If you want, remember the man on the lane, and let there be no one to step aside from. The bell holds the time.
Jnana yoga, and its four qualifications: viveka, telling lasting from passing; vairagya, dispassion; six treasures of a steady mind; and “mumukshutva”, the longing to be free.

Your line: who am I? Today, when you catch yourself sizing someone up by what they look like or what they do, remember the lane in Kashi, and ask which should move from which. Day two hundred seventy-seven.

trapdoor: what you thought: the knowledge path is for clever people.

what a scholar hears: the fourfold qualification (sadhana chatushtaya) and the six treasures (shama, dama, uparati, titiksha, shraddha, samadhana) are set out in Vivekachudamani and Tattvabodha; the Manisha Panchakam story comes from later hagiographies (Shankara-digvijaya).

278.title: Jnana yoga: neti neti in practice; Shankara's method; the Ashtavakra Gita opening (5 of 7)
278.hook: a boy bent in eight places walks into a king's court, and the court laughs
278.tomorrow: Jnana yoga: neti neti in practice; Shankara's method; the Ashtavakra Gita opening (6 of 7)
278.howItsDone: The Ashtavakra Gita is read and chanted in many Advaita circles as a direct statement of non-dual teaching, often studied alongside the Upanishads; its opening questions from King Janaka frame the whole text.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the lane in Kashi, and the four qualifications. Discernment, dispassion, a steady mind, longing to be free. Your line: who am I? Did you catch yourself sizing someone up? Day two hundred seventy-eight.

The Mahabharata tells of a scholar named Kahoda who recited the Vedas while his wife was pregnant. From inside the womb, the unborn child corrected his father's mistakes. Eight times. The father, embarrassed and furious, cursed him: you'll be born bent in eight places. And he was. They called him Ashtavakra: eight bends. Years later, Kahoda lost a debate at the court of King Janaka and never came home. And the boy, twelve years old, crooked and limping, set out for that court to win his father back.
screen: `CORRECTED FROM THE WOMB.` → `ASHTAVAKRA: EIGHT BENDS.` → `A BOY GOES TO THE KING'S COURT.`

segments.voice: In the Mahabharata's telling, the boy talks his way past the gatekeeper, then defeats the court's champion debater, and his father is restored. There's a popular addition people love to tell: when Ashtavakra walked in, the courtiers laughed at his body, and he laughed back. Why are you laughing? they asked. And he said: I thought this was an assembly of the wise. It's a gathering of leather-workers. You only judge the skin. Whether that exchange is old or newer, it fits the book that carries his name. The Ashtavakra Gita is a short Sanskrit dialogue between the sage and King Janaka. Nobody knows when it was written. Scholars guess anywhere from about the eighth to the fourteenth century, later than the Mahabharata story it draws on. But it's become one of the most loved texts of the jnana path, precisely because it's so blunt. It opens with the king asking three questions. Paraphrased: how is knowledge gained? How will freedom come? And how is detachment reached? Tell me this, my lord. Three questions. Not how do I become a better person. Not how do I get to heaven. How do I know. How am I free. How do I let go. That's the whole jnana path in one breath. Notice who's asking, too. A king, with everything. In the Upanishads, Janaka is the model of someone who lives in the world, rules it well, and isn't owned by it. And the answer he gets, tomorrow, doesn't ask him to give up his throne.
screen: `THE COURT LAUGHS AT THE BODY.` · `YOU ONLY JUDGE THE SKIN.` · `A KING ASKS THREE QUESTIONS.` · `KNOWLEDGE, FREEDOM, LETTING GO.` · then, large: `WHO AM I?`

segments.voice: Sit, and ask Janaka's three questions for yourself, slowly, one per stretch of breathing. First: what do I actually know, for certain, right now? Stay with it. Then: where do I feel not free? Just notice, no fixing. Then: what am I gripping? A plan, a person, an idea of myself. Let each question open, and don't rush an answer. The asking is the practice. The bell holds the time.
Jnana yoga, through the Ashtavakra Gita: a dialogue between a sage bent in eight places and King Janaka, who asks how to know, how to be free, how to let go.
Your line: who am I? Today, notice one moment when you judge someone by the skin, their looks, their clothes, their accent, and look again. Day two hundred seventy-eight.

what it means: he's the sage of a famous non-dual dialogue with King Janaka, the Ashtavakra Gita.

279.title: Jnana yoga: neti neti in practice; Shankara's method; the Ashtavakra Gita opening (6 of 7)
279.hook: a king asks for a long path; the sage says: right now
279.tomorrow: Jnana yoga: neti neti in practice; Shankara's method; the Ashtavakra Gita opening (7 of 7)
279.howItsDone: Students of the Ashtavakra Gita often chant or read its first chapter slowly, pausing on each verse, and use its list of the five elements as a contemplation: noticing each as known, and resting as the knower.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ashtavakra, the sage of eight bends, and King Janaka's three questions. How do I know? How am I free? How do I let go? Your line: who am I? Today, the answer. Day two hundred seventy-nine.

Most of us assume anything worth having takes a long time. Learning an instrument: years. Getting in shape: months of mornings. So when a king asks how to be free, you'd expect a long program. Twelve years in a forest. A thousand rules. A ladder with a hundred rungs. Ashtavakra's answer starts gently enough, with a little advice about how to live. And then, a few verses in, it says something so bold you may read the line twice to be sure you got it.
screen: `WORTH HAVING TAKES A LONG TIME.` → `A KING ASKS HOW TO BE FREE.` → `THEN THE ANSWER GETS BOLD.`

segments.voice: Here's the opening of Ashtavakra's reply, paraphrased. If you want freedom, my child, treat the pull of the senses like poison, and drink forgiveness, honesty, kindness, contentment and truth like nectar. That's the gentle part. A good life, sensibly described. Then the next verse turns everything. You are not earth. You are not water, or fire, or air, or space. To be free, know yourself as the witness of all these: awareness itself. Neti neti again, in the king's own language. The old Indian list of five elements that make up everything, and the sage says: you're none of them. You're the one they appear to. Then the verse that stops people. If you set the body aside and rest in awareness, then right now, this very moment, you'll be happy, at peace, and free. Right now. Not after twelve years. Not after you've fixed your temper or your diet. Now. A little later he adds: right and wrong, pleasure and pain, belong to the mind, not to you. You're not the doer. You're not the one who enjoys the results. You were always free. Is that too easy? Teachers in the tradition say it isn't easy at all; it's simple, which is different. Nothing has to be built. But everything you keep counting as yourself has to be seen through, the way the leader by the river had to stop counting and turn around. That's why the Ashtavakra Gita is so loved on the jnana path. It doesn't give you a ladder. It points at the floor you're already standing on.
screen: `SENSES AS POISON, VIRTUES AS NECTAR.` · `YOU ARE NOT EARTH, WATER, FIRE.` · `THE WITNESS OF ALL THESE.` · `RIGHT NOW: HAPPY, AT PEACE, FREE.` · then, large: `WHO AM I?`

segments.voice: Sit, and walk Ashtavakra's list slowly. Earth: the weight of the body on the seat. Not what I am; something I notice. Water: the moisture in the mouth. Noticed. Fire: the warmth of the skin. Noticed. Air: the breath. Noticed. Space: the room around you. Noticed. Then, for a few breaths, rest as the one noticing, right now. Not later. If the mind says it's not working, that's a thought. Noticed. The bell holds the time.
Jnana yoga, in the Ashtavakra Gita's answer: you are not the elements, but the witness of them, awareness itself; rest there, and you're free now.
Your line: who am I? Today, when you're sure something has to be fixed before you can be at peace, try one breath of Ashtavakra's right now. Day two hundred seventy-nine.

280.title: Jnana yoga: neti neti in practice; Shankara's method; the Ashtavakra Gita opening (7 of 7)
280.hook: think you're bound, and you are; think you're free, and you are
280.tomorrow: Advaita (Shankara): not-two; rope and snake in full; the Vivekachudamani opening (1 of 7)
280.howItsDone: Many Hindu teachers present karma, bhakti and jnana (often with raja yoga, meditation) as paths suited to different temperaments, while also teaching that they support one another; the Bhagavad Gita is the classic text that holds all three.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ashtavakra's bold answer. You are not the elements, but their witness; rest there, and you're free now. Your line: who am I? Today, the last day of jnana, and of the three paths. Day two hundred eighty.

You've seen it happen. Two people get the same bad news, the same layoff, the same diagnosis. One says: that's it, I'm finished. The other says: all right, what now? The facts are identical. What they take themselves to be is not. And over the next year, you can watch the two stories come true. There's an old Indian saying about this, and the Ashtavakra Gita puts it right in its first chapter, in a verse many people know by heart.
screen: `THE SAME BAD NEWS.` → `I'M FINISHED. OR: WHAT NOW?` → `BOTH STORIES COME TRUE.`

segments.voice: The verse, paraphrased: whoever takes themselves to be free is free, and whoever takes themselves to be bound is bound. The saying is true: as you think, so you become. Ya matih sa gatih. Where the mind goes, there you go. In the Ashtavakra Gita this isn't positive thinking. It's not about talking yourself into a good mood. It's about identity. If you take yourself to be the body, the job, the moods, you'll feel bound by all of them. If you know yourself as the witness, the chains were never locked. That's the end of our jnana week. Neti neti, not this, not this. The tenth man who forgot to count himself. Maitreyi, who turned down the fortune, and Shankara's hearing, reflecting, soaking in. The lane in Kashi. The boy with eight bends. And today: as you think, so you become. It's also the end of three weeks on the three paths. Karma: offer the work. Bhakti: love as the road. Jnana: who am I? Some teachers present them as separate roads suited to different temperaments, the doer, the lover, the thinker. Vivekananda did, and added a fourth, raja yoga, the path of meditation. Others say they braid together, and point to the Gita, which weaves all three through its eighteen chapters. Hindus disagree, happily, about which road to lean on. Nobody here is asking you to choose. You've walked a stretch of each. Next, the path goes deeper into two great schools, starting with the one that says: not two.
screen: `FREE IF YOU TAKE YOURSELF AS FREE.` · `AS YOU THINK, SO YOU BECOME.` · `THE DOER, THE LOVER, THE KNOWER.` · `THREE ROADS, OFTEN BRAIDED.` · then, large: `WHO AM I?`

segments.voice: Sit, and try the three paths in one sit. First, karma: think of one piece of work waiting for you, and offer it. Then bhakti: bring to mind someone or something you love, and let the warmth rise. Then jnana: turn around and ask, quietly, who is offering, who is loving? Don't answer. Just rest as the one who's asking. If a sense of freedom comes, let it. If it doesn't, that's fine too. The bell holds the time.
Jnana yoga, the path of knowledge: knowing yourself as the witness. Its closing verse: whoever takes themselves as free is free. As you think, so you become.
Your line: who am I? Today, when you hear yourself say I'm stuck, or I'm hopeless, ask whether that's what you are, or something passing through. Day two hundred eighty.

fork.setup: two friends lose their jobs the same week. one says: I'm finished. the other: what now? by Ashtavakra's verse, what makes the difference?

fork.reveal: whoever takes themselves as bound is bound; whoever takes themselves as free is free. as you think, so you become.

original.note: Sanskrit: 'as the mind, so the destination' — the saying quoted in Ashtavakra Gita 1.11.

trapdoor: what you thought: as you think, so you become is a self-help slogan.
what it means: in the Ashtavakra Gita, it's about what you take yourself to be: bound, or the free witness.
what a scholar hears: Ashtavakra Gita 1.11 calls it a true popular saying (kimvadantīha satyeyam); the idea that one's final thought shapes one's destination also appears in the Gita (8.6).
